📊 Ad Campaign Engagement: Preprocessing & EDA¶

Team Project Notebook

Objective: Prepare our ad dataset for predicting engagement_duration (Regression task) and analyze how our features are distributed so we can build the right neural network architecture.

1. Data Preprocessing¶

First, we need to clean up the raw data. In this step, we will:

  1. Drop irrelevant identifiers: user_id, ad_id, and interaction_timestamps don't help our neural net.
  2. Keep TF-IDF: We are leaving the tfidf columns untouched because they represent the actual text content of the ads, which is crucial for predicting engagement.
  3. Reorder: Move our target variable (conversion) to the very end of the dataframe for convenience.
  4. Optional Normalization: There is a block of code at the end that applies Min-Max scaling to continuous features. You can comment it out if you want to run baseline models on raw numbers first.
In [2]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

# 1. Load the original dataset
df = pd.read_csv('ad_campaign_data.csv')

# 2. Drop unnecessary identifiers and timestamps
columns_to_drop = ['user_id', 'ad_id', 'interaction_timestamps']
df_processed = df.drop(columns=columns_to_drop)

# 3. Normalization
continuous_features = ['age', 'impressions', 'clicks', 'previous_interaction_score', 'sentiment_score']
scaler = MinMaxScaler()
df_processed[continuous_features] = scaler.fit_transform(df_processed[continuous_features])

print(f"Processed dataset shape: {df_processed.shape}")
df_processed.head()

2. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Let's visualize the distributions of our continuous and categorical features to understand the shape of our data before feeding it into the neural network.

In [3]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Set up the visual style
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

# Define our feature groups
continuous_features = ['age', 'impressions', 'clicks', 'engagement_duration', 'previous_interaction_score', 'sentiment_score']
categorical_features = ['gender', 'location', 'device_type', 'ad_category', 'conversions']

# --- Plot 1: Continuous Distributions ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 10))
fig.suptitle('Distributions of Continuous Features', fontsize=16)
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, col in enumerate(continuous_features):
    sns.histplot(df[col], kde=True, ax=axes[i], bins=30, color='skyblue')
    axes[i].set_title(col)
    axes[i].set_xlabel('')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# --- Plot 2: Categorical Distributions ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 10))
fig.suptitle('Distributions of Categorical Features', fontsize=16)
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, col in enumerate(categorical_features):
    val_counts = df[col].value_counts().sort_index()
    sns.barplot(x=val_counts.index, y=val_counts.values, ax=axes[i], palette='Set2')
    axes[i].set_title(col)
    axes[i].set_xlabel('Category')
    axes[i].set_ylabel('Count')

axes[5].set_visible(False) # Hide the last empty subplot
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# --- Plot 3: Correlation Matrix for Continuous Features ---
continuous_df = df_processed[continuous_features] # dataframe with continuous features
sns.heatmap(continuous_df.corr(), annot=True, vmin=-1, vmax=1, center=0, cmap='coolwarm', linewidths=0.5, linecolor='black', square=True)
plt.title('Correlation Matrix for Continuous Features', fontsize=16)
plt.show()

# --- Plot 4: Pairplot ---

pairplot_features.append('conversions')
pairplot_df = df_processed[pairplot_features]
sns.set_style('whitegrid')
sns.pairplot(pairplot_df, hue='conversions')
plt.show()

3. Yeo-Johnson Transformation¶

Because the distribution of clicks is right skewed, we apply Yeo-Johnson transformation to make the distribution more normal. This will allow us to get better results for our SVM and Naïve Bayes models. The Yeo-Johnson distribution is good for exponential distributions and works with 0 and negative values.

In [36]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

df_transformed = df.copy()
# Drop columns we're not using
df_transformed.drop(columns=columns_to_drop, inplace=True)
# Apply Yeo-Johnson transformation to clicks to reduce right skew
transformer = PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson')
df_transformed['clicks'] = transformer.fit_transform(df_transformed[['clicks']])

# Visualize change in distribution
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))
# Clicks before transformation
axes[0].hist(df_processed['clicks'], bins=50, color="steelblue", edgecolor="white")
axes[0].set_title("Clicks (Raw)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Clicks")
# Clicks after transformation
axes[1].hist(df_transformed['clicks'], bins=50, color="darkorange", edgecolor="white")
axes[1].set_title("Clicks (Yeo-Johnson Transformed)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Clicks (Transformed)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Apply min-max normalization after transformation
continuous_features = ['age', 'impressions', 'clicks', 'previous_interaction_score', 'sentiment_score']
scaler = MinMaxScaler()
df_transformed[continuous_features] = scaler.fit_transform(df_transformed[continuous_features])

4. One-Hot Encoding for Categorical Features¶

Because the numbers assigned to the categorical features are arbitrary, we use one-hot encoding to prevent bias in our models.

Variables to Be One-Hot Encoded: gender, location, device_type, and ad_category conversions is not encoded since it is our predictor.

For the Naïve Bayes model, we can't use one-hot encoding because the features are assumed to be independent. We use label encoding instead. The categorical features are already label encoded.

In [37]:
# One-hot encode the categorical features
encode_vars = ['gender', 'location', 'device_type', 'ad_category']
df_encoded = pd.get_dummies(df_processed, columns=encode_vars, prefix=encode_vars, dtype=int)
# For SVM model (with transformed clicks)
df_encoded_svm = pd.get_dummies(df_transformed, columns=encode_vars, prefix=encode_vars, dtype=int)

# Move the target variable ('conversions') to the end
encoded_feature_cols = [col for col in df_encoded.columns if col != 'conversions']
df_encoded = df_encoded[encoded_feature_cols + ['conversions']]
df_encoded_svm = df_encoded_svm[encoded_feature_cols + ['conversions']]

# Save to a clean CSV for the team to use
output_filename = 'final_project_data.csv'
df_encoded.to_csv(output_filename, index=False)
df_encoded_svm.to_csv('svm_project_data.csv', index=False)

# Save data without one-hot encoding to a clean CSV for the Naïve Bayes model
processed_feature_cols = [col for col in df_processed.columns if col != 'conversions']
df_nb = df_transformed[processed_feature_cols + ['conversions']]
df_nb.to_csv('nb_project_data.csv', index=False)

# Move the target variable ('conversions') to the end
print(f"Encoded dataset shape: {df_encoded.shape}")
df_encoded.head()

5. Key Feature Notes & Analysis for the Team¶

Based on the EDA plots generated above, here are the main takeaways for our model architecture:

Continuous Features¶

  • Uniformity: Age, Impressions, Engagement Duration, Previous Interaction Score, and Sentiment Score are almost perfectly uniformly distributed.
  • Skewness: Clicks is the only continuous feature with a natural-looking right-skewed distribution (a long tail to the right). Most ads have fewer clicks, while a select few have extremely high numbers.
  • Correlation: Most of the features are uncorrelated, except for Clicks and Impressions

Categorical Features¶

  • Perfectly Balanced Demographics: Gender (~50/50), Location (~20% across 5 zones), Device Type (~33% across 3 types), and Ad Category (~20% across 5 types) are incredibly well-balanced.
  • Highly Imbalanced Conversions: About 89.8% of users converted, while only 10.2% did not. Since this is out target, this may cause bias in our models.
